readings.title: The mission, vision, and invitation
paragraphs: Welcome to Discover Your Divine Design
Discover how God designed you to live. On Purpose. For Purpose.

You were not created randomly. You were formed intentionally and invited into meaningful work. Rooted in Ephesians 2:10, Discover Your Divine Design is a guided journey of Scripture and reflection that helps you recognize who you already are, by design.
“For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.” Ephesians 2:10
The Mission & Vision Behind DYDD
Mission: On Purpose
Discover Your Divine Design exists to help people rediscover who they are in Christ. Scripture tells us that we are God’s workmanship, His masterpiece, created intentionally and uniquely by Him.

Through biblical teaching, reflection, and practical tools, DYDD helps people gain clarity about their identity, story, gifts, and design so they can live with confidence in who God created them to be.
“For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus…”— Ephesians 2:10
Vision: For Purpose
We envision a Church where believers understand their design and joyfully participate in the work God has prepared for them.
When people discover their identity and embrace their unique contribution, they find belonging, meaningful service, and a deeper sense of calling within the Body of Christ.
“…to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.”— Ephesians 2:10
Discover Your Divine Design helps believers understand how God uniquely created them so they can live and serve with clarity and purpose.
The DYDD Journey

Discover Your Divine Design equips believers to understand how God has uniquely shaped their life, gifts, and passions for meaningful service. This journey walks through six core areas that bring clarity and confidence so you can live On Purpose, For Purpose.

readings.title: The theology of design and hoped-for outcomes
paragraphs: Ephesians 2:8-10 and the Theology of Design
Saved by Grace – Designed on Purpose - Walking in the Good Works Prepared for Us

“For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast. For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.” Ephesians 2:8–10

Discover Your Divine Design begins with the truth of this passage. Ephesians 2:8–10 reveals the full story of the Christian life. It shows how salvation begins, how God forms His people, and how He intends them to live. These verses remind us that our relationship with God begins with grace, continues through His intentional design, and unfolds through the good works He prepared for us long before we ever recognized them.
DYDD is built around this movement. We are saved by grace, designed on purpose, and invited to walk in the good works God prepared for us.
Saved by Grace

The foundation of everything begins with grace. Salvation is not something we achieve through effort, talent, or accomplishment. It is a gift from God. We are brought into relationship with Him through faith, not through our own performance or ability.

This truth protects the entire journey of discovering our design. Purpose is not about earning God's approval or proving our value. Instead, it grows from the security of knowing we already belong to Him. When people understand they are saved by grace, they are free to explore how God created them without pressure, comparison, or striving.
Designed on Purpose
Ephesians continues by reminding us that we are God's handiwork. The word used in this passage points to something carefully crafted, something formed with intention and care.

Every believer has been uniquely shaped by God. Our story, identity, experiences, abilities, desires, and spiritual gifts all reflect aspects of how He formed us. Discover Your Divine Design helps people recognize this intentional design. Rather than seeing their life as random or disconnected, participants begin to see how God has been shaping them for meaningful contribution.
Walking in Good Works Prepared for Us
The passage ends with a powerful reminder. God not only saves and shapes us, He prepares a path for us to walk.

Good works are not something we invent for ourselves. Scripture tells us that God prepared them in advance. Our role is to recognize where He is leading and step into those opportunities with faith and obedience.

This is the heart of the DYDD journey. As people understand their design, they begin to see where their life can serve others, strengthen the church, and reflect the work God is already doing around them. Discovering our design is not the final goal. The goal is to live faithfully in the good works God has prepared for us.
What Churches Can Expect from the DYDD Journey

Discover Your Divine Design is designed to help believers recognize how God has uniquely shaped them and where their lives can contribute to His work. When a church walks through this journey together, participants begin to see themselves and one another through a new lens. Rather than simply asking where help is needed, people begin to understand how their God given design can serve the body of Christ and the world around them.

Churches that lead the DYDD journey often see several meaningful outcomes. Individuals gain greater clarity about how God has formed them and where their life naturally contributes. Participants begin to connect their story, identity, abilities, desires, and spiritual gifts in ways that help them recognize patterns of design they had not noticed before. This process often brings renewed confidence, deeper spiritual reflection, and a greater willingness to step into service.

The journey also strengthens the life of the church. As people understand their design, they often become more engaged in ministry and more intentional in how they serve. Leaders gain insight into the diversity of gifts and contributions present within the congregation. Ministries can begin to align people more thoughtfully with opportunities where they are most likely to flourish.

Another important outcome is a culture of encouragement and discovery. Conversations during the journey allow participants to affirm what they see in one another. As people share their experiences and insights, the community begins to recognize the many ways God is working through different individuals. This mutual encouragement helps believers step forward with greater confidence in how God may use them.

The goal of DYDD is not simply to complete a study or identify a label. The goal is to help believers recognize how God has designed them and to begin living more intentionally within the good works He has prepared for them. As participants move forward in faith, the church often sees people serving with renewed joy, deeper purpose, and a clearer understanding of their role within the body of Christ.

steps.title: See the whole journey
steps.subtitle: Eight sessions. One unfolding discovery.

essentials.title: Follow the path, not the acronym
paragraphs: Identity → Expertise → Story → Desire → Spiritual Gifts → Niche. DESIGN is a way to remember the elements, not their teaching order. Identity in Christ comes first so the remaining discoveries rest on belonging rather than striving.

The opening session establishes the foundation. The final two gatherings stay distinct: Session 7 brings the pieces together in Niche preparation; Session 8 makes room for declarations, affirmation, commissioning, and next steps.

essentials.title: Let the pieces build
paragraphs: Identity asks whose we are. Expertise notices developed abilities. Story brings context and perspective. Desire notices what stirs our heart. Spiritual Gifts explores Spirit-empowered service. Niche brings these into contact with opportunities to serve.
A niche is not a permanent job title. It is an emerging place of contribution, tested through faithfulness, community, and experience.

essentials.title: Use CARE as a rhythm, not more homework
paragraphs: Connect, Act, Reflect, Explore: engage with God and others, take a faithful step, pause to notice what is happening, and remain curious about what God may be opening.

Participants use their own digital workbook and Field Kit. They decide which insights to bring into conversation. A private “Bring to discussion” reminder does not send a reflection or note to you or the group.

readings.title: The elements of DESIGN
paragraphs: D.E.S.I.G.N.

Design is used as an acronym to represent the process taken for Discovery. It is not completed in the order of the acronym, on purpose. The process was carefully developed to help participants build from section to section, constantly gaining ground in their understanding.

The DYDD journey helps participants explore six key areas of their life that together reveal how God has uniquely shaped them. Each element offers a different perspective on how God forms a person through identity, experiences, passions, and spiritual empowerment. As participants reflect on these areas, they often begin to see patterns that reveal how their design may connect with the good works God has prepared for them.
Identity

It all begins with knowing whose you are. Before we can understand what we are called to do, we must first understand who we are in Christ. Identity provides the foundation for the entire journey because our sense of purpose flows from our relationship with God and the truth of what He says about us.
Participants often find themselves reflecting on questions such as:
Have I been carrying labels that do not reflect God’s truth about me?
What does Scripture reveal about my identity in Christ?
How might seeing myself through God’s perspective change the way I live and serve?
Expertise

It all builds with what you have learned. Over time, each person develops knowledge, skills, and practical experience through work, education, relationships, and daily responsibilities. These abilities may feel ordinary to the person who possesses them, yet they often represent important ways God has been preparing them to contribute to others.
Participants begin recognizing that:
Skills they once considered routine may actually hold meaningful value
Strengths developed over time can become tools for serving others
God often prepares people for purpose through everyday experiences
Story

It all comes together through your story. Every person carries a unique set of life experiences that shape perspective, compassion, and understanding. As participants reflect on their story, they often begin to see how God has been present and active throughout different seasons of their life.
This reflection may reveal:
Experiences that shaped their perspective or strengthened their faith
Difficult seasons that now provide empathy and understanding for others
Moments where God’s guidance becomes clearer in hindsight
Desire

It all deepens with what stirs your heart. God often places interests, passions, and concerns within us that draw our attention toward particular needs or opportunities. These desires can provide important clues about where our design may naturally find expression.
Participants may begin noticing:
Interests or passions that consistently capture their attention
Problems or needs that move them toward action
Opportunities that feel both meaningful and energizing
Spiritual Gifts

It all strengthens when God equips you. Spiritual gifts represent the ways the Holy Spirit empowers believers to serve and build up the Body of Christ. These gifts extend beyond natural talents and reflect God’s grace working through His people.
As participants explore this area, they may begin discovering:
Ways God has already been working through them to encourage or strengthen others
Spiritual strengths that become evident through service and community
Opportunities to use these gifts more intentionally within the life of the church
Niche

It all leads to where your design meets God’s purpose. Niche represents the intersection where identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts begin to align with real opportunities to serve others. Rather than defining a permanent role, niche reflects a growing awareness of how a person’s design can make a meaningful contribution.
Participants often begin asking:
Where do the different elements of my design naturally come together?
Who might God be inviting me to serve?
What opportunities around me could become expressions of purpose?
Bringing the Elements Together

As these six elements begin to connect, participants often discover that their life carries a clearer sense of direction. What once seemed like unrelated experiences, abilities, and passions begins forming a unified design. Over time, this awareness helps individuals step forward with greater confidence, recognizing that God has been shaping their life all along for the good works He prepared in advance for them to do.

readings.title: How the framework leads to discovery
paragraphs: Understanding the Journey of Discovery

The Discover Your Divine Design journey is structured to guide participants through a thoughtful process of reflection and discovery. Each section builds on the one before it, helping individuals gradually recognize how God has shaped their life and how those elements work together.

The process begins with Identity. Before exploring gifts, skills, or calling, it is important to establish a clear foundation in who we are in Christ. When people understand their identity in Him, they can approach the rest of the journey from a place of security rather than striving.

From there the journey moves to Expertise. Many people overlook the ways God has been shaping them through education, experience, and skill development. This section helps participants recognize that the abilities they have developed throughout life often become important tools God uses in their contribution.

Story follows next. Our experiences, both joyful and difficult, often shape how we understand people, problems, and opportunities. Looking back through the lens of faith helps participants see how God may have been preparing them in ways they had not previously recognized.

The journey then turns toward Desire. As people reflect on what stirs their heart, they often begin to notice patterns of interest and concern that reveal where their energy and compassion naturally rise. These desires frequently point toward areas where individuals feel most alive serving others.

Finally, the process explores Spiritual Gifts. Scripture teaches that the Holy Spirit empowers believers to serve the body of Christ in specific ways. Recognizing these gifts provides another important layer of understanding as participants begin to see how God may work through them to bless others.
Each section adds clarity, gradually revealing how the different aspects of a person’s life come together to form a meaningful pattern of design.
How the Process Leads to Discovery

The goal of this journey is not to rush participants toward a quick answer about their purpose. Instead, the process creates space for thoughtful reflection, conversation, and prayer. As individuals move through each section, they begin to recognize connections between the different parts of their design.

Identity provides the foundation. Expertise reveals developed abilities. Story offers context and perspective. Desire highlights where the heart is drawn. Spiritual Gifts reveal ways the Spirit empowers service.

When these pieces are considered together, participants begin to see patterns that may have been hidden before. What once felt like unrelated parts of life start to form a clearer picture. Skills connect with experiences. Passions align with opportunities. Gifts begin to illuminate areas where God may be inviting someone to serve.

Discovery often happens gradually. Participants may recognize certain aspects of their design quickly, while other insights may take time to develop. The conversations, reflections, and exercises throughout the journey are designed to help people notice these connections and consider how God might be guiding them forward.

By the end of the process, many participants begin to see where their design naturally intersects with the needs around them. This intersection becomes the starting point for understanding their niche and exploring how they can live more intentionally in the good works God has prepared for them.
Why Niche

The goal of the DYDD journey is not simply self-understanding. It is participation in the work God is already doing. The concept of Niche helps bring the different parts of a person’s design together so they can begin to see where their life most naturally serves others.

A niche is the place where identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts begin to intersect. It is not a title or a position. It is the environment where a person’s design aligns with opportunities to serve and make an impact.

Many believers want to live with greater purpose but are unsure how their life fits into the larger work of God’s Kingdom. Exploring a niche helps move the conversation from general calling to practical expression. It helps people recognize where their design may be most effective and where their contribution can be most meaningful.

Understanding a niche does not mean every question about the future is answered. Instead, it provides direction. It gives individuals a clearer starting point for stepping forward in faith and exploring how God may use their life in the good works He has prepared.

readings.title: CARE and the assessment journey
paragraphs: Introducing the C.A.R.E. Process

Throughout the Discover Your Divine Design journey, participants are encouraged to move beyond simply reading or discussing the material. The goal is to create space for reflection, prayer, conversation, and application. To support this process, the DYDD workbook uses a simple framework called C.A.R.E.

C.A.R.E. stands for Connect, Act, Reflect, and Explore. These four movements help participants engage more deeply with what they are learning and how God may be shaping their understanding of their design.

Connect invites participants to engage with God, themselves, and the people around them. This may happen through prayer, conversation, or personal reflection as individuals begin noticing where God has been shaping their story and stirring their heart.

Act encourages participants to take small, faithful steps in response to what they are discovering. Instead of waiting until every answer feels clear, participants are invited to move forward with trust, applying insights as they continue learning.

Reflect creates space to pause and consider what is happening throughout the journey. Participants are encouraged to notice patterns, evaluate what they are learning, and discern where God may be leading them next.

Explore invites curiosity and openness. Participants ask questions, imagine possibilities, and consider how God might be inviting them to grow beyond what they previously understood about their life and contribution.

Leaders should encourage participants to use the C.A.R.E. process as they move through the workbook exercises. These prompts help individuals slow down and thoughtfully process each section of the journey.

The DesignID assessment is a central part of the DYDD journey. It is designed to help participants recognize their core reflection and contribution style within the body of Christ. While many assessments focus only on personality or behavior, DesignID explores how a person naturally contributes within community and ministry.

The assessment identifies one of four primary reflections that represent different ways people often express their design. These reflections provide insight into how individuals tend to approach vision, truth, people, and stewardship. Understanding this reflection helps participants see how they may naturally contribute within teams, ministries, and leadership environments.

Participants typically complete the DesignID assessment early in the journey during the Identity section. The results provide a helpful lens through which participants can explore the rest of the process. As individuals move through expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts, the DesignID insights help them better understand how these elements interact with their natural reflection and contribution style.

The Spiritual Gifts Assessment helps participants recognize the ways the Holy Spirit equips believers to serve others. Scripture teaches that the Spirit distributes gifts within the body of Christ so that the church can function and grow together. This assessment provides a structured way for participants to identify possible areas where the Spirit may be empowering their service.

Participants complete the Spiritual Gifts Assessment later in the journey after reflecting on identity, expertise, story, and desire. This timing allows them to consider their gifts within the broader context of how God has shaped their life. The goal is not to assign a permanent label but to help individuals recognize patterns of gifting that can be confirmed through scripture, community affirmation, and real-life service.

Together these resources help participants move through the DYDD journey in a thoughtful and practical way, gradually bringing clarity to how their design may align with the good works God has prepared for them.
As groups work through the book, participants will see a C.A.R.E. icon that directs them to continue the process in the workbook.

steps.title: Create room for discovery
steps.subtitle: Guide the process. Don’t supply everyone’s answers.

essentials.title: You are a guide, not the expert on someone else’s life
paragraphs: Introduce the main idea, ask a thoughtful question, and leave room for people to reflect. You do not have to interpret each person’s design or resolve every uncertainty.
Model humility. “I don’t know yet; let’s keep noticing and praying” is an honest response. Help people connect evidence from life and service, Scripture, and community rather than assign a calling.

essentials.title: Build trust before asking for depth
paragraphs: Learn names, welcome people warmly, and explain that listening matters as much as speaking. Ask permission before drawing someone into the conversation. Passing is always an option.
Agree not to retell one another’s personal stories outside the Circle. Being in the same Circle does not grant access to private workbook answers, discussion notes, or assessment details.

essentials.title: Make conversation balanced
paragraphs: Ask one clear question, give people time to think, then listen without rushing to advice. Invite another voice when one person has taken most of the time.

If the room drifts into comparison, correction, or debate, return to curiosity: “What are you beginning to notice in your own life?” Specific situations and suggested wording are in the Leader Toolkit.

steps.action: Choose one sentence you will use to establish the Circle’s culture, and one question that invites reflection without demanding disclosure.

readings.title: Who can host
paragraphs: Who Should Host the DYDD Journey

The Discover Your Divine Design journey can be hosted by a variety of leaders within the church. The most important factor is not the title of the leader but the commitment to guide people through the process with care and encouragement.

Many churches choose to host DYDD through small group ministries, discipleship programs, leadership development initiatives, or adult education classes. Pastors, ministry leaders, small group leaders, or trusted facilitators can all serve effectively in guiding the journey.

The host should be someone who is comfortable leading discussion, encouraging participation, and helping people reflect on what they are learning. They do not need to be experts in the material. The role of the host is to create a welcoming environment where participants can explore how God has designed them and how their lives may contribute to His work.

Churches may choose to have one primary facilitator or a small team of leaders who guide the experience together. In either case, the goal is to provide steady leadership and a consistent environment where participants can move through the journey with confidence.

readings.title: Community and discovery
paragraphs: The Role of Community in Discovering Design

Discovering how God has designed a person is rarely a journey meant to be taken alone. While reflection and personal insight are important, the process becomes much richer when it takes place within a community. When participants walk through the DYDD journey together, they have the opportunity to listen to one another, share experiences, and recognize patterns of design that might otherwise go unnoticed.

A healthy environment for this journey begins with leaders and participants who are willing to truly hear and see one another. Each person brings a different story, background, and level of spiritual maturity. Some participants may be exploring these ideas for the first time, while others may already have years of ministry or leadership experience. Creating space where every person is valued and respected allows individuals to share openly and learn from one another.

Walking through the process as a cohort also builds meaningful relationships. As participants discuss their story, reflect on their experiences, and consider how God has shaped their life, they often discover common themes and shared encouragement. These conversations create connections that extend beyond the class itself, forming relationships that can continue to provide support and accountability as individuals begin living out their design.

The wider church community also plays an important role in this journey. When the church embraces the idea that every believer has been intentionally designed by God, it opens the door for people to explore where they may serve and contribute. As more members participate in the DYDD journey, the church develops a shared language around design, purpose, and contribution. This shared understanding helps leaders and participants alike recognize new opportunities for involvement, allowing people to step forward, serve, and grow as they continue discovering the good works God has prepared for them.

readings.title: Facilitating meaningful discussions
paragraphs: The Role of the Facilitator

The facilitator plays an important role in guiding participants through the DYDD journey. This role is less about teaching expertise and more about creating an environment where people can reflect, share, and discover how God has been shaping their life.

A facilitator helps guide the rhythm of each session by introducing the main ideas, encouraging conversation, and allowing space for participants to process what they are learning. Rather than providing all the answers, the facilitator helps participants ask thoughtful questions and notice the ways God may already be at work in their life.

The goal of the facilitator is to create a setting where individuals feel seen, heard, and valued. As participants share their reflections, the facilitator helps maintain a respectful and encouraging atmosphere where people can speak openly and listen well to one another.
Scripture reminds leaders that growth within the church happens as people are equipped and encouraged to serve.

“So Christ himself gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the pastors and teachers, to equip his people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up.”Ephesians 4:11–12 (NIV)

In this sense, the facilitator serves as a guide who helps participants move through the journey of discovery. By encouraging reflection, conversation, and prayer, facilitators help individuals begin recognizing how God has designed them and where He may be inviting them to serve.
Key Concepts for Facilitators
Facilitators guide the process rather than control it. The DYDD journey works best when participants are given time to think, reflect, and speak for themselves.

Listening is one of the most important leadership skills in this role. Participants often gain clarity as they share their insights with others, so creating space for thoughtful conversation is essential.

Facilitators should encourage curiosity and reflection rather than trying to interpret someone’s design for them. The goal is to help participants discover how God has been shaping their life, not to assign conclusions.
Facilitators should also model humility and openness. When leaders approach the journey with curiosity and faith, it helps participants feel comfortable doing the same.
Areas Facilitators Should Watch For

Facilitators should be mindful of participants who may dominate conversation as well as those who may hesitate to speak. Encouraging balanced participation helps ensure everyone has the opportunity to share.

It is also important to watch for moments when discussions drift toward giving advice rather than listening. The purpose of the conversations is to explore and reflect, not to correct or direct someone else’s journey.

Facilitators should gently redirect conversations that move into comparison or judgment. Each participant’s design and story are unique, and the goal is to celebrate that diversity rather than measure one person against another.
Encouraging a posture of respect, curiosity, and prayer throughout the journey helps create the environment where participants can engage deeply and grow together.
Creating a Culture of Discovery

One of the most important responsibilities of a leader during the DYDD journey is helping cultivate an environment where discovery can take place. Participants will be reflecting on personal experiences, spiritual questions, and areas of growth, so the overall culture of the group should be welcoming, supportive, and respectful.

A healthy culture of discovery begins with hospitality. Participants should feel that they are entering a space where they are valued and where their voice matters. Simple practices such as greeting people warmly, learning names, and encouraging conversation help create an atmosphere where individuals feel comfortable engaging with the material and with one another.

Trust is also essential. Many of the conversations throughout the DYDD journey invite participants to reflect on personal experiences and spiritual growth. When people feel safe to share honestly without fear of judgment or comparison, they are much more likely to engage deeply in the process. Leaders can support this environment by modeling humility, listening carefully, and responding with encouragement.

Another important element of a discovery culture is curiosity. Participants should be reminded that the goal of the journey is not to arrive at perfect answers but to explore how God has been shaping their life. Questions, reflection, and thoughtful discussion are part of the process. When curiosity is welcomed, participants often begin noticing connections in their story and design that they had not previously considered.

A nurturing environment also encourages mutual support within the group. As participants listen to one another’s experiences and insights, they begin to recognize the many ways God is working through different individuals. This shared discovery strengthens relationships and helps participants appreciate the diversity of gifts and perspectives within the body of Christ.
Scripture reminds us that growth in faith often happens within community.
“Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.”1 Thessalonians 5:11 (NIV)

When a culture of encouragement and discovery is present, participants are more likely to engage honestly, support one another, and remain open to the ways God may be shaping their understanding throughout the journey.
Leading Effective Table Discussions

Table discussions are one of the most important parts of the DYDD journey. While teaching introduces the concepts, conversation is often where participants begin recognizing how those ideas connect to their own life. As individuals listen to one another, share reflections, and ask questions, they often discover insights that might not emerge through reading or teaching alone.

Leaders should view table discussions as an essential part of the learning process rather than simply an optional activity. These conversations allow participants to process what they are learning in community, which often leads to deeper understanding and stronger relationships within the group.

Effective table discussions begin with clear and simple questions. Prompts should invite reflection rather than demand perfect answers. Questions that begin with phrases such as “What stood out to you,” “Where have you seen this in your life,” or “What are you beginning to notice” help participants engage naturally with the conversation.

Facilitators should also encourage balanced participation. Some individuals are comfortable speaking quickly, while others need time to think before sharing. A healthy discussion environment allows space for both. Leaders can gently invite quieter participants to share while also guiding the conversation so that no one voice dominates the group.

Listening is one of the most valuable skills during table discussions. Participants should be encouraged to listen carefully to one another without immediately offering advice or correction. Often the most helpful response is simply acknowledging what someone has shared and allowing the group to reflect together.
Scripture reminds us that wisdom often grows through listening and thoughtful conversation.
“My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry.”James 1:19 (NIV)

Leaders should also help keep conversations aligned with the purpose of the session. Discussions may occasionally drift into unrelated topics or personal debates. When this happens, facilitators can gently guide the group back to the reflection questions and the purpose of the session.

Table discussions are not meant to produce perfect conclusions. Their purpose is to help participants reflect on their experiences, recognize patterns in their design, and learn from the insights of others. When conversations remain respectful, curious, and encouraging, these moments often become some of the most meaningful parts of the entire journey.
Helping Participants Process Their Design

As participants move through the DYDD journey, they will begin noticing patterns in their identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts. Processing these insights thoughtfully is an important part of the experience. Leaders play a helpful role by guiding participants as they reflect on what they are learning and how the different pieces of their design begin to connect.

Participants often need time to recognize how the various elements of their life fit together. Rather than rushing toward conclusions, leaders should encourage a posture of reflection, prayer, and curiosity. The goal is not to force a quick answer about purpose but to help individuals notice the ways God may already be shaping their life and inviting them forward.

The workbook plays an important role in this process. The C.A.R.E. reflections help participants slow down and engage with what they are learning. By connecting, acting, reflecting, and exploring, individuals begin to see how their experiences, abilities, and spiritual gifts interact with one another. Leaders should regularly encourage participants to revisit their workbook reflections as they process their design.

It is also helpful for participants to discuss their insights with others in the group. Hearing how others perceive their strengths or contributions can often provide confirmation or clarity that individuals may not see on their own. These conversations reinforce the biblical picture of the church as a community where believers help one another grow.
Scripture reminds us that wisdom and understanding often develop through counsel and shared insight.
“Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.”Proverbs 15:22 (NIV)

Leaders should remind participants that discovering their design is not about creating a perfect description of who they are. Instead, it is about recognizing how God has been shaping their life and beginning to walk faithfully in the direction He is leading.

Processing design also requires humility and openness. Some participants may initially struggle to recognize their strengths, while others may discover aspects of their design they had not previously considered. Encouraging participants to hold their insights with both gratitude and curiosity helps keep the journey focused on growth rather than certainty.

Ultimately, the role of the leader is to help participants see connections. As identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts begin to align, individuals often gain a clearer picture of how their life may contribute to the body of Christ and to the good works God has prepared for them.
Common Questions and How to Respond

As participants move through the DYDD journey, it is natural for questions to arise. Many individuals are exploring aspects of their life and faith in ways they may not have considered before. Leaders should welcome these questions and approach them with patience, humility, and encouragement.

The role of the leader is not to provide every answer but to help guide participants toward thoughtful reflection, prayer, and conversation. Many questions are best explored within community rather than solved immediately.
Several types of questions commonly arise during the journey.

Some participants may ask whether they have identified their purpose correctly. It is helpful to remind them that the goal of the journey is not to produce a final answer but to begin recognizing patterns in how God has shaped their life. Purpose often becomes clearer as individuals continue walking in obedience.
Scripture reminds us that God guides His people step by step.
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.”Proverbs 3:5–6 (NIV)

Others may wonder if their design seems too ordinary or unimportant. Leaders can encourage participants by reminding them that God works through everyday faithfulness. Many of the most meaningful contributions within the church happen through simple acts of service, encouragement, and leadership.
“Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much.”Luke 16:10 (NIV)

Some participants may feel uncertain about their assessment results or struggle to see how the different parts of their design fit together. Leaders should encourage them to view the assessments and reflections as tools for discovery rather than final conclusions. Insight often grows over time through prayer, experience, and the affirmation of others in community.

There may also be participants who compare their design with others in the group. Leaders should gently remind the group that diversity is an intentional part of God’s design for the church. Each person contributes in a different way, and every role is valuable.
“Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.”1 Corinthians 12:27 (NIV)

Finally, some individuals may feel hesitant about taking a next step. They may worry about making the wrong decision or moving in the wrong direction. Leaders can reassure participants that God often leads through small steps of faithfulness rather than immediate clarity about the entire path.
Encouraging participants to remain prayerful, attentive, and open to God’s guidance helps them approach the journey with confidence and humility.

The purpose of responding to questions is not to resolve every uncertainty but to help participants remain engaged in the process of discovery. As they continue reflecting, serving, and walking with God, clarity about their design and contribution will often grow naturally over time.

readings.title: Structure and resources
paragraphs: Recommended Class Structure

Discover Your Divine Design is designed to be flexible so churches can adapt the experience to their own context. The journey can be offered in a variety of formats such as weekly gatherings, monthly sessions, small groups, leadership cohorts, or virtual environments. The most important element is not the schedule but the process participants move through together.

The class should follow the order of the journey presented in the book and workbook. Participants move through the sections in this sequence: Identity, Expertise, Story, Desire, and Spiritual Gifts. Each step builds on the one before it, helping individuals gradually recognize how the different parts of their life and design fit together.

The workbook provides the primary structure for reflection and discovery. Participants should be encouraged to complete the workbook exercises as they move through each section. These reflections help individuals process what they are learning and prepare them for meaningful discussion during the group sessions.

Conversation is an essential part of the experience. Each gathering should allow time for table discussions where participants can share insights, ask questions, and reflect together. These table talks often become the most valuable part of the journey as people begin to hear how God has been working in one another’s lives.

Throughout the journey, each session should gradually point toward the final outcome of the process. As participants explore each section, leaders can help them notice how the different elements begin to connect. By the time the group reaches the final stages of the journey, participants are prepared to see how their design leads toward their niche, the place where their life most naturally aligns with the good works God has prepared for them.

readings.title: Common launch mistakes
paragraphs: Common Launch Mistakes
Common Launch Mistakes Churches Should Avoid

Introducing the DYDD journey into a church can become a powerful catalyst for helping believers discover and live out their design. Like any new initiative, however, the way it is introduced can influence the long-term impact it will have within the congregation.
The following insights can help leaders avoid common challenges as they begin implementing the DYDD process.
Trying to Rush the Process

The DYDD journey is designed to guide participants through reflection, discussion, and discovery. When leaders try to move too quickly through the material, participants may understand the concepts but miss the deeper personal insights that come through thoughtful reflection.

Encourage participants to take time with the exercises, conversations, and assessments. Clarity often develops gradually as individuals process their experiences and begin recognizing patterns in their design.
Treating the Course as Information Instead of Transformation
The goal of DYDD is not simply to teach new ideas but to help believers recognize how God has shaped them and how their lives can contribute to the work of His Kingdom.

Leaders should create an environment where participants feel comfortable sharing their experiences and exploring their design honestly. Discussion, reflection, and prayer are often just as important as the teaching itself.
Focusing Only on Church Roles

While the church provides many opportunities for service, God’s design for a person’s life extends far beyond formal ministry roles. Participants should be encouraged to recognize how their design influences their work, relationships, community involvement, and daily interactions.
Purpose often appears in ordinary environments where faithfulness and service are lived out over time.
Neglecting the Follow Up
One of the most important moments in the DYDD journey occurs after the class concludes. Participants may leave the course feeling inspired but unsure about their next steps.

Simple follow up conversations, mentoring relationships, or invitations to serve can help individuals move from insight into action. These small moments of encouragement often make a significant difference in helping participants continue exploring their purpose.
Allowing the Journey to End with the Class

DYDD is most effective when it becomes part of an ongoing culture within the church rather than a one-time course. Alumni gatherings, mentoring relationships, and continued conversations about design help keep the journey alive within the community.
When churches continue creating environments where people explore their design and support one another, the impact of the DYDD journey multiplies over time.

readings.title: Facilitation — full guidance
paragraphs: The Role of the Facilitator

The facilitator plays an important role in guiding participants through the DYDD journey. This role is less about teaching expertise and more about creating an environment where people can reflect, share, and discover how God has been shaping their life.

A facilitator helps guide the rhythm of each session by introducing the main ideas, encouraging conversation, and allowing space for participants to process what they are learning. Rather than providing all the answers, the facilitator helps participants ask thoughtful questions and notice the ways God may already be at work in their life.

The goal of the facilitator is to create a setting where individuals feel seen, heard, and valued. As participants share their reflections, the facilitator helps maintain a respectful and encouraging atmosphere where people can speak openly and listen well to one another.
Scripture reminds leaders that growth within the church happens as people are equipped and encouraged to serve.

“So Christ himself gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the pastors and teachers, to equip his people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up.”Ephesians 4:11–12 (NIV)

In this sense, the facilitator serves as a guide who helps participants move through the journey of discovery. By encouraging reflection, conversation, and prayer, facilitators help individuals begin recognizing how God has designed them and where He may be inviting them to serve.
Key Concepts for Facilitators
Facilitators guide the process rather than control it. The DYDD journey works best when participants are given time to think, reflect, and speak for themselves.

Listening is one of the most important leadership skills in this role. Participants often gain clarity as they share their insights with others, so creating space for thoughtful conversation is essential.

Facilitators should encourage curiosity and reflection rather than trying to interpret someone’s design for them. The goal is to help participants discover how God has been shaping their life, not to assign conclusions.
Facilitators should also model humility and openness. When leaders approach the journey with curiosity and faith, it helps participants feel comfortable doing the same.
Areas Facilitators Should Watch For

Facilitators should be mindful of participants who may dominate conversation as well as those who may hesitate to speak. Encouraging balanced participation helps ensure everyone has the opportunity to share.

It is also important to watch for moments when discussions drift toward giving advice rather than listening. The purpose of the conversations is to explore and reflect, not to correct or direct someone else’s journey.

Facilitators should gently redirect conversations that move into comparison or judgment. Each participant’s design and story are unique, and the goal is to celebrate that diversity rather than measure one person against another.
Encouraging a posture of respect, curiosity, and prayer throughout the journey helps create the environment where participants can engage deeply and grow together.
Creating a Culture of Discovery

One of the most important responsibilities of a leader during the DYDD journey is helping cultivate an environment where discovery can take place. Participants will be reflecting on personal experiences, spiritual questions, and areas of growth, so the overall culture of the group should be welcoming, supportive, and respectful.

A healthy culture of discovery begins with hospitality. Participants should feel that they are entering a space where they are valued and where their voice matters. Simple practices such as greeting people warmly, learning names, and encouraging conversation help create an atmosphere where individuals feel comfortable engaging with the material and with one another.

Trust is also essential. Many of the conversations throughout the DYDD journey invite participants to reflect on personal experiences and spiritual growth. When people feel safe to share honestly without fear of judgment or comparison, they are much more likely to engage deeply in the process. Leaders can support this environment by modeling humility, listening carefully, and responding with encouragement.

Another important element of a discovery culture is curiosity. Participants should be reminded that the goal of the journey is not to arrive at perfect answers but to explore how God has been shaping their life. Questions, reflection, and thoughtful discussion are part of the process. When curiosity is welcomed, participants often begin noticing connections in their story and design that they had not previously considered.

A nurturing environment also encourages mutual support within the group. As participants listen to one another’s experiences and insights, they begin to recognize the many ways God is working through different individuals. This shared discovery strengthens relationships and helps participants appreciate the diversity of gifts and perspectives within the body of Christ.
Scripture reminds us that growth in faith often happens within community.
“Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.”1 Thessalonians 5:11 (NIV)

When a culture of encouragement and discovery is present, participants are more likely to engage honestly, support one another, and remain open to the ways God may be shaping their understanding throughout the journey.
Leading Effective Table Discussions

Table discussions are one of the most important parts of the DYDD journey. While teaching introduces the concepts, conversation is often where participants begin recognizing how those ideas connect to their own life. As individuals listen to one another, share reflections, and ask questions, they often discover insights that might not emerge through reading or teaching alone.

Leaders should view table discussions as an essential part of the learning process rather than simply an optional activity. These conversations allow participants to process what they are learning in community, which often leads to deeper understanding and stronger relationships within the group.

Effective table discussions begin with clear and simple questions. Prompts should invite reflection rather than demand perfect answers. Questions that begin with phrases such as “What stood out to you,” “Where have you seen this in your life,” or “What are you beginning to notice” help participants engage naturally with the conversation.

Facilitators should also encourage balanced participation. Some individuals are comfortable speaking quickly, while others need time to think before sharing. A healthy discussion environment allows space for both. Leaders can gently invite quieter participants to share while also guiding the conversation so that no one voice dominates the group.

Listening is one of the most valuable skills during table discussions. Participants should be encouraged to listen carefully to one another without immediately offering advice or correction. Often the most helpful response is simply acknowledging what someone has shared and allowing the group to reflect together.
Scripture reminds us that wisdom often grows through listening and thoughtful conversation.
“My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry.”James 1:19 (NIV)

Leaders should also help keep conversations aligned with the purpose of the session. Discussions may occasionally drift into unrelated topics or personal debates. When this happens, facilitators can gently guide the group back to the reflection questions and the purpose of the session.

Table discussions are not meant to produce perfect conclusions. Their purpose is to help participants reflect on their experiences, recognize patterns in their design, and learn from the insights of others. When conversations remain respectful, curious, and encouraging, these moments often become some of the most meaningful parts of the entire journey.
Helping Participants Process Their Design

As participants move through the DYDD journey, they will begin noticing patterns in their identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts. Processing these insights thoughtfully is an important part of the experience. Leaders play a helpful role by guiding participants as they reflect on what they are learning and how the different pieces of their design begin to connect.

Participants often need time to recognize how the various elements of their life fit together. Rather than rushing toward conclusions, leaders should encourage a posture of reflection, prayer, and curiosity. The goal is not to force a quick answer about purpose but to help individuals notice the ways God may already be shaping their life and inviting them forward.

The workbook plays an important role in this process. The C.A.R.E. reflections help participants slow down and engage with what they are learning. By connecting, acting, reflecting, and exploring, individuals begin to see how their experiences, abilities, and spiritual gifts interact with one another. Leaders should regularly encourage participants to revisit their workbook reflections as they process their design.

It is also helpful for participants to discuss their insights with others in the group. Hearing how others perceive their strengths or contributions can often provide confirmation or clarity that individuals may not see on their own. These conversations reinforce the biblical picture of the church as a community where believers help one another grow.
Scripture reminds us that wisdom and understanding often develop through counsel and shared insight.
“Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.”Proverbs 15:22 (NIV)

Leaders should remind participants that discovering their design is not about creating a perfect description of who they are. Instead, it is about recognizing how God has been shaping their life and beginning to walk faithfully in the direction He is leading.

Processing design also requires humility and openness. Some participants may initially struggle to recognize their strengths, while others may discover aspects of their design they had not previously considered. Encouraging participants to hold their insights with both gratitude and curiosity helps keep the journey focused on growth rather than certainty.

Ultimately, the role of the leader is to help participants see connections. As identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts begin to align, individuals often gain a clearer picture of how their life may contribute to the body of Christ and to the good works God has prepared for them.
Common Questions and How to Respond

As participants move through the DYDD journey, it is natural for questions to arise. Many individuals are exploring aspects of their life and faith in ways they may not have considered before. Leaders should welcome these questions and approach them with patience, humility, and encouragement.

The role of the leader is not to provide every answer but to help guide participants toward thoughtful reflection, prayer, and conversation. Many questions are best explored within community rather than solved immediately.
Several types of questions commonly arise during the journey.

Some participants may ask whether they have identified their purpose correctly. It is helpful to remind them that the goal of the journey is not to produce a final answer but to begin recognizing patterns in how God has shaped their life. Purpose often becomes clearer as individuals continue walking in obedience.
Scripture reminds us that God guides His people step by step.
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.”Proverbs 3:5–6 (NIV)

Others may wonder if their design seems too ordinary or unimportant. Leaders can encourage participants by reminding them that God works through everyday faithfulness. Many of the most meaningful contributions within the church happen through simple acts of service, encouragement, and leadership.
“Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much.”Luke 16:10 (NIV)

Some participants may feel uncertain about their assessment results or struggle to see how the different parts of their design fit together. Leaders should encourage them to view the assessments and reflections as tools for discovery rather than final conclusions. Insight often grows over time through prayer, experience, and the affirmation of others in community.

There may also be participants who compare their design with others in the group. Leaders should gently remind the group that diversity is an intentional part of God’s design for the church. Each person contributes in a different way, and every role is valuable.
“Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.”1 Corinthians 12:27 (NIV)

Finally, some individuals may feel hesitant about taking a next step. They may worry about making the wrong decision or moving in the wrong direction. Leaders can reassure participants that God often leads through small steps of faithfulness rather than immediate clarity about the entire path.
Encouraging participants to remain prayerful, attentive, and open to God’s guidance helps them approach the journey with confidence and humility.

The purpose of responding to questions is not to resolve every uncertainty but to help participants remain engaged in the process of discovery. As they continue reflecting, serving, and walking with God, clarity about their design and contribution will often grow naturally over time.

readings.title: Frequently asked questions
paragraphs: Frequently Asked Questions — The following questions often arise as participants begin the DYDD journey.
What if I am not sure what my purpose is yet?

The goal of the DYDD journey is not to produce a perfect answer about purpose. Instead, the course helps participants begin recognizing patterns in how God has shaped their life. Purpose often becomes clearer as individuals continue serving and growing.
Do I have to take the assessments?

The DesignID and Spiritual Gifts assessments are valuable tools for reflection, but participation is ultimately optional. Many participants find the assessments helpful for recognizing patterns in their design, but the most important insights often come through reflection, prayer, and conversation.
What if my results do not feel accurate?

Assessments provide helpful insight, but they are not final declarations. Participants should view the results as starting points for reflection. Over time, experiences in service and encouragement from others often help confirm or refine what participants discover.
What if I do not feel like I have strong gifts or abilities?

Every believer contributes uniquely to the body of Christ. Sometimes individuals simply have not yet recognized the ways God has shaped them. As participants reflect on their story, experiences, and spiritual gifts, many begin to see contributions they previously overlooked.
What happens after the course ends?

The DYDD journey is intended to begin a process of discovery rather than complete it. Participants are encouraged to continue reflecting on their design, exploring opportunities to serve, and seeking guidance from mentors and leaders as they grow in their understanding of purpose.

readings.title: Common launch mistakes
paragraphs: Common Launch Mistakes
Common Launch Mistakes Churches Should Avoid

Introducing the DYDD journey into a church can become a powerful catalyst for helping believers discover and live out their design. Like any new initiative, however, the way it is introduced can influence the long-term impact it will have within the congregation.
The following insights can help leaders avoid common challenges as they begin implementing the DYDD process.
Trying to Rush the Process

The DYDD journey is designed to guide participants through reflection, discussion, and discovery. When leaders try to move too quickly through the material, participants may understand the concepts but miss the deeper personal insights that come through thoughtful reflection.

Encourage participants to take time with the exercises, conversations, and assessments. Clarity often develops gradually as individuals process their experiences and begin recognizing patterns in their design.
Treating the Course as Information Instead of Transformation
The goal of DYDD is not simply to teach new ideas but to help believers recognize how God has shaped them and how their lives can contribute to the work of His Kingdom.

Leaders should create an environment where participants feel comfortable sharing their experiences and exploring their design honestly. Discussion, reflection, and prayer are often just as important as the teaching itself.
Focusing Only on Church Roles

While the church provides many opportunities for service, God’s design for a person’s life extends far beyond formal ministry roles. Participants should be encouraged to recognize how their design influences their work, relationships, community involvement, and daily interactions.
Purpose often appears in ordinary environments where faithfulness and service are lived out over time.
Neglecting the Follow Up
One of the most important moments in the DYDD journey occurs after the class concludes. Participants may leave the course feeling inspired but unsure about their next steps.

Simple follow up conversations, mentoring relationships, or invitations to serve can help individuals move from insight into action. These small moments of encouragement often make a significant difference in helping participants continue exploring their purpose.
Allowing the Journey to End with the Class

DYDD is most effective when it becomes part of an ongoing culture within the church rather than a one-time course. Alumni gatherings, mentoring relationships, and continued conversations about design help keep the journey alive within the community.
When churches continue creating environments where people explore their design and support one another, the impact of the DYDD journey multiplies over time.

readings.title: On Purpose, For Purpose
paragraphs: Session 1 — On Purpose, For Purpose

This opening session sets the foundation for the entire DYDD journey. Before participants explore the different aspects of their design, it is important that they understand the central truth guiding the process. God creates people intentionally and invites them to live with purpose within His Kingdom.

The session introduces the core theme of the journey: On Purpose, For Purpose. Participants are reminded that their life is not accidental and that God has been shaping them long before they began considering questions of calling or contribution. This conversation is rooted in Ephesians 2:8–10, which explains that believers are saved by grace, formed by God as His handiwork, and invited to walk in the good works He prepared in advance.
“For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.”Ephesians 2:10 (NIV)

This first gathering helps participants understand that discovering their design is not about striving to earn significance. Instead, it is about recognizing how God has already been shaping their life and learning to walk faithfully in what He has prepared.
Key Concepts for Leaders

Participants need to hear clearly that purpose grows out of grace. The DYDD journey does not ask people to manufacture purpose or prove their value. It invites them to recognize the work God is already doing in their life.

It is also helpful to emphasize that purpose unfolds over time. Many people enter the journey hoping for a single clear answer about their calling. Leaders can gently remind participants that clarity often develops gradually as they reflect, serve, and continue walking with God.
Relevant scripture passages can help reinforce this understanding.
Jeremiah 29:11 reminds believers that God has intentions for their future.
“For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the Lord, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.”Jeremiah 29:11 (NIV)
Psalm 139 affirms the intentional way God forms each life.
“For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother’s womb.”Psalm 139:13 (NIV)
Areas Leaders Should Watch For

Some participants may struggle with feelings that their life has lacked purpose. Others may carry disappointment from past experiences that seemed to contradict their expectations of how God would lead them. Leaders should create a welcoming environment where people can acknowledge these feelings without pressure to resolve them immediately.

Another common challenge is comparison. Participants may begin measuring their design against the gifts or experiences of others in the group. Leaders should regularly remind the group that the goal of the journey is not to rank or compare designs but to recognize the unique ways God works through each person.
Encouraging participants to listen carefully to one another and celebrate the diversity within the group helps create a healthy environment for discovery.
Discussion Focus
The primary goal of this session is to help participants begin asking a simple but important question.
What if God has been shaping my life on purpose?

Allow time for participants to reflect on where they may already see signs of God’s intentional work in their life. These early conversations begin preparing the group for the deeper exploration that will unfold throughout the rest of the journey.
Session 2 — Identity and the DesignID Assessment

This session focuses on the foundation of identity. Before participants explore how they serve or where they contribute, it is essential that they understand who they are in Christ. Identity shapes how people see themselves, how they relate to others, and how they interpret their role within the body of Christ.

The conversation begins with the biblical truth that identity is not formed by performance, achievement, or comparison. Identity is established through relationship with Christ. When believers understand whose they are, they are able to approach questions of purpose and contribution with humility, freedom, and confidence.

readings.title: Identity and DesignID — full session guidance
paragraphs: “So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith.”Galatians 3:26 (NIV)

This session also introduces the DesignID assessment. DesignID is a tool that helps participants recognize how their identity and contribution tend to express themselves within community and ministry. Rather than measuring personality traits or preferences alone, the assessment highlights patterns of reflection and contribution that often shape how a person engages with others and participates in the work of the church.

The DesignID results identify one of four primary reflections that represent different ways people naturally contribute. These reflections help participants recognize the lens through which they often see problems, opportunities, and relationships. Understanding this reflection gives participants language for how their design may show up in leadership, service, teamwork, and ministry environments.

Participants are encouraged to complete the DesignID assessment during this stage of the journey. The insights gained from the report will serve as a helpful framework as they continue exploring expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts in the sessions that follow.
Key Concepts for Leaders

Identity must remain rooted in Christ, not in an assessment result. DesignID is a helpful tool for reflection and insight, but it should never replace the deeper truth of who a person is as a child of God.

Leaders should emphasize that the assessment provides language for understanding tendencies, not labels that limit a person. The goal is to help participants notice patterns in how God has shaped them so they can better understand their contribution within the body of Christ.
Another important concept is the diversity of design within the church. Scripture teaches that the body of Christ is made up of many different parts, each contributing in unique ways.
“Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.”1 Corinthians 12:27 (NIV)
When participants begin to see how their reflection differs from others in the group, it often creates appreciation for the variety of ways God works through His people.
Areas Leaders Should Watch For

Some participants may place too much importance on the assessment result. Leaders should remind the group that DesignID is simply a tool that helps bring language to what may already be present in their life and experiences.

Others may struggle if their result feels unexpected or unclear. Encourage participants to read the report thoughtfully and discuss their insights with others in the group. Often, community conversation helps confirm and clarify what the assessment reveals.

Leaders should also watch for comparison. Participants may be tempted to view certain reflections as more valuable or more spiritual than others. Scripture reminds us that every role within the body of Christ is important and necessary.
Discussion Focus
This session invites participants to consider two important questions.
What does it mean for my identity to be rooted in Christ?
How might the way God designed me influence how I contribute to the body of Christ?
These conversations help participants begin recognizing how their identity and reflection provide a foundation for the rest of the DYDD journey.
DesignID Overview

DesignID is introduced during the Identity portion of the DYDD journey because it helps participants understand how their identity often expresses itself in community, leadership, and service. While identity in Christ forms the spiritual foundation of who we are, DesignID provides helpful language for recognizing how our design tends to show up in real life.

The assessment helps participants identify patterns in how they perceive situations, process information, relate to others, and contribute to the work of the church. Rather than defining a person or limiting their potential, DesignID offers insight into natural tendencies that often shape how individuals engage with people, opportunities, and challenges.

As participants move through the remaining sections of the DYDD journey, the DesignID insights serve as a helpful lens for understanding how their expertise, story, desires, and spiritual gifts may combine to influence their contribution.

The goal of introducing DesignID at this stage is not to analyze every detail of the report. Instead, it simply helps participants begin recognizing how God may have uniquely shaped their perspective and contribution within the body of Christ.
DesignID Elements Overview:
Element
What it is
Why it matters
Reflections
Reflections identify the primary way a person tends to see the world and respond to opportunities, challenges, and relationships.
Understanding a reflection helps participants recognize how they naturally contribute within teams, ministries, and leadership environments.
Integrative Reflections
Integrative reflections describe how two reflections often work together to shape a person’s broader perspective and approach to collaboration.
These integrations help participants see how their design may bridge different perspectives within the body of Christ.
Capacity
Capacity describes the current level of energy and strength a person has available within each reflection.
Recognizing capacity helps participants understand where they may currently operate with strength, balance, or limitation and encourages healthy stewardship of their energy.
Approaches to Learning
This area describes how individuals often prefer to learn, process information, and grow in understanding.
Understanding learning tendencies helps participants develop in ways that align with how they naturally absorb and apply new insight.
Contribution to the Body
This portion of the report highlights how a person’s reflection often expresses itself within the body of Christ.
It helps participants recognize how their design supports the work of the church and complements the contributions of others.
Shadow Reflections
Shadow reflections describe potential distortions that may appear when a person’s strengths become overextended or unbalanced.
Recognizing these shadows helps participants grow in humility and awareness, allowing their strengths to remain healthy and life giving within community.
